title: Open–Closed Principle
summary: A module should be open for extension but closed for modification, so adding a new case adds code instead of editing it.
signals: the same type switch repeated across files (a fee calculator and a refund-message builder both branch on the same enum)
a code-review comment saying "you also need to update the switch in the other file"
a bug where one branch of a type switch was updated and a sibling switch elsewhere was not
adding a new case to a domain concept requires editing several existing classes instead of adding one new one

roles.CancellationFeeCalculator (before): one switch on order type, duplicated logic that must stay in sync with a second switch elsewhere
roles.RefundDescription (before): a second switch on the same order type, patched independently of the fee switch and now out of sync
roles.FeePolicy (after): the extension point — one small interface every order type implements
roles.StandardFeePolicy / ExpressFeePolicy / C: one policy per existing type, each owning its own fee and refund description
roles.CancellationFeeCalculator (after): chooses a policy from a map by order type; adding a type means adding an entry, not a branch

stages.title: One switch, then a second one
stages.idea: CancellationFeeCalculator branches on order.type to compute the fee; RefundDescription branches on the same order.type for the customer-facing message, but was never updated when custom-made orders were added.

stages.title: One policy per type, chosen once
stages.idea: Each order type is a FeePolicy owning both its fee and its refund description; the calculator picks one from a map. A new type is a new policy added to the map — no existing file changes.

checks: In the before code, what already-shipped bug shows that duplicating a type switch is worse than duplicating ordinary code? Why does it stay hidden until someone reads both switches side by side?

"Closed for modification" cannot mean "never edit this code again" — the after stage's calculator was written once and never touched to add the gift policy. State what specifically stays unedited when a new order type is added, and what is allowed to change.

Meyer's original open-closed principle relied on inheritance-based extension; Martin's version prefers implementing an interface plumbed in through composition. What does the after stage's FeePolicy map buy over subclassing CancellationFeeCalculator for each order type?

If cancellation fees only ever had one order type in production and a second was purely hypothetical, would introducing FeePolicy before a second type exists be a good application of this principle? Why or why not?
